name: Wei Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day in the kitchen look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wei, 27, and I have a vocational cooking certificate. I lead lunch in a busy restaurant, set the chicken board apart, check the fridge and call plates out over the noise. I like a clean service, but my flat rate is low and I have only two weeks of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cooks AI Plateau sounds like another till update. We still have to get lunch out hot and keep raw chicken away from salad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run the lunch serving counter, but the owner pays a small flat rate and I've got about two weeks of bills saved. A dull Tuesday already means someone loses a shift; I don't want to gamble on a new system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll keep the lunch checks on paper and ask for the December rota before the rent date. I'll set aside a little from any paid Sunday cover after rent, food and fares, instead of buying a new jacket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about hours, not the small software change. Knowing how to cook doesn't make a short rota longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check on paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mark raw chicken boards and the fridge temperatures before lunch. If a screen prints a wrong allergy note, I still ask the server to confirm with the guest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save Sunday money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday cover is the only shift that sometimes gives me anything spare. I will not count it until the money actually lands.

say: I'd tell cooks **ordinary AI** changes a till, while lunch still needs safe hands.
I'd keep **raw chicken** apart from salad regardless of what a screen says.
think: My **flat rate** and two-week reserve make a lost lunch shift expensive.
I prefer **paper checks** I can see during the rush.
do: Keep **lunch safety checks** and request the written December rota.
Save **cleared Sunday-cover pay** after rent, food and fares.
feel: I feel **anxious** about thin savings and short rotas.
S0.quote: Knowing how to cook doesn't make a short rota longer.
fieldNote: His **senior lunch skill** coexists with a low flat rate and only two weeks saved.
His **paper checks** cover chicken boards and fridge temperatures, not a rejection of food-safety records.

steps.text: Keep lunch checks on paper and request the December rota
Save cleared Sunday-cover pay after rent, food and fares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner Steady Disruption may handle bookings and orders, but it must not guess whether a guest can eat sesame. I would keep a cook and a server checking each change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the booking software fills fewer tables, my flat wage could get cut. I use no AI tools now, and I won't start trusting one because the office calls it efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask the owner to show the revised paid rota and who signs allergy changes, then keep taking my booked lunch shifts. If my shifts fall, I'll look at posted senior-cook work nearby, but leave only for a signed offer my certificate and experience meet, with net pay after bus fares replacing my full current weekly take-home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because our dining room could empty a bit and there aren't many other kitchens hiring. At least I know what a real weekly payslip looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you refuse the booking screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the printed booking list, but a human server must confirm the allergy with the guest. I would stop a plate if the answer was unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about a new restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check its actual posted hours and late bus first. A better title means nothing if I lose money getting home.

say: I'd tell the **owner** that software can book tables while cooks still verify dangerous allergies.
I'd keep a **human server** confirming guest details before food leaves.
think: Fewer **paid shifts** could hit my small reserve if software changes booking patterns.
I do not **trust AI tools** without a person checking the actual guest order.
do: Request the **revised paid rota** and named allergy sign-off.
Seek **posted senior-cook work** after cuts; leave only for a qualified signed net replacement after bus fares.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a thinner rota and few local openings.
S1.quote: A better title means nothing if I lose money getting home.
fieldNote: He will **read bookings** but does not commit to adopting an AI tool himself.
A **new kitchen** needs an actual opening, his certificate accepted and signed net pay after bus fares.

steps.text: Request revised paid rota and human allergy sign-off; keep booked lunch shifts
Seek posted qualified senior-cook role after cuts; leave for signed replacement net pay after bus fares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lunch crew AGI by 2028 could change orders and staff lists almost at once, but cooking robots are about three years behind. A machine still won't be holding the frying pan in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the owner to strip our paid ordering and prep time, because that is easier than buying a robot. That could be a big part of my small wage, and I've been waking at four thinking about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll get my current paid hours and duties written down now and ask when any 2028 cuts start. In the first year after AGI arrives, I'll keep cooking while the shifts pay; if prep hours are cut, I'll apply for a posted school-kitchen cook job only if my certificate and safe-food experience meet its requirements, and move only after a signed net offer after travel replaces my full current weekly take-home and the hours fit the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed by the pay I expect to lose, though I'm not giving up the serving counter. The knife work and food checks are still ours until capable robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a school kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A school still has meals and allergy rules, but I don't know if it will post a paid opening. I can't leave this restaurant on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep the paid shifts left here and cancel the jacket purchase. I won't pay for a course just because a website promises jobs.

say: I'd tell the **crew** that AGI changes orders by 2028, while cooking robots follow around 2031.
I'd insist **food checks** and hot pans still have named human responsibility.
think: Likely lost **prep hours** would remove a large share of my small wage.
I wake early over **rent** because my reserve covers only two weeks.
do: Document **paid prep duties** and ask about any planned 2028 changes.
Apply **posted paid school cook** after cuts; require accepted certificate/experience, signed full-weekly-net replacement after travel and workable shift bus.
Keep **paid restaurant shifts** until that signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by expected income loss and broken sleep.
S2.quote: A machine still won't be holding the frying pan in 2028.
fieldNote: His **alarm** concerns expected paid prep cuts, not an invented 2028 robot chef.
A **school kitchen** is a conditional search requiring a real vacancy, qualification, workable bus and signed net pay.

steps.text: Document paid prep duties and ask about any planned 2028 changes
Apply after cuts for posted paid school cook; require certificate/experience, signed full net-after-travel replacement/bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to get wages and duties clear. The stove and lifting stay human work until robots around 2034, so I'd want the owner to price those hours honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could hold the lunch serving counter for years, but a longer warning doesn't guarantee a full rota. I have two weeks saved and no taste for betting rent on a shiny course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask for a written pay review for the lunch lead duties and keep a log of actual covers and safety checks. In the first year after 2031 I'll stay if the signed shifts still pay the bills; if paid hours fall, I'll apply to a posted hotel breakfast-lead role only when my certificate and service experience qualify, the early bus works and the written net pay after fares replaces my full current weekly take-home; I'll keep this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though the extra time makes a careful search possible. I want a payslip I can read, not a promise that the future will need cooks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why breakfast rather than another lunch line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is an early bus and I know how to turn out hot plates quickly. I still need an actual vacancy and written wage before calling it a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the employer funds the recognised place and study time is paid without dropping my current wages. I won't buy a certificate the hotel doesn't accept.

say: I'd tell the **team** that planning changes by 2031 while capable cooking robots follow around 2034.
I'd ask the **owner** to price human lifting, cooking and safety hours clearly.
think: The **longer warning** does not guarantee my lunch rota or bill money.
My **two-week reserve** cannot finance a speculative training course.
do: Request a **written lunch-lead review** and record covers and safety checks.
Seek **posted paid breakfast cook** after cuts; require accepted certificate/experience, signed full net-after-fares replacement and early bus; retain current job.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to search carefully over several years.
S3.quote: I want a payslip I can read, not a promise that the future will need cooks.
fieldNote: His **wage review** uses documented lunch leadership and safety work, not a speculative new business.
A **hotel move** requires reduced current hours, a posted qualified vacancy, early transport and signed net replacement pay.

steps.text: Request written lunch-lead pay review and log covers and safety checks
Seek posted paid breakfast cook after cuts; require certificate/experience, signed full net-after-fares replacement/early bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team AGI by 2036 is a decade away, while cooking robots follow around 2039. I would rather spend the decade getting decent pay for people at the stove than guessing what a robot kitchen looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I may still be a cook with a mortgage or a family, and I don't know which. Two weeks of savings now won't carry me through a bad winter, never mind a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the lunch serving counter and ask for an annual written rate review based on actual covers. I'll put a small share of cleared Sunday cover pay into a three-month bill fund after rent, food and fares; in the first year after 2036 I'll keep taking paid human shifts and review the real rota before any job move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The distance makes the robots feel less immediate, but my current low rate still makes me anxious. Ten years is useful only if I get paid enough along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the rate never rises?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count nearby posted cook vacancies and their bus times, then compare written net wages. I won't quit a paid shift for a nicer job title with no signed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the long warning useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real wage rise and three months of bills saved would give me choices. I don't need an AI lesson to tell me when chicken is cooked safely.

say: I'd say **2036 AGI** changes planning before capable cooking robots arrive around 2039.
I'd press for **decent stove wages** during the long warning.
think: A possible **future family** makes long-term pay matter, though I cannot predict it.
My **two-week reserve** makes the coming winter risky already.
do: Keep the **lunch pass** and request an annual written rate review, including after 2036.
Save **cleared Sunday pay** toward three months' bills after rent, food and fares.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current pay despite distant robots.
S4.quote: Ten years is useful only if I get paid enough along the way.
fieldNote: His **long horizon** does not justify assuming a future family or funded retirement income.
His **practical plan** is a rate review, current shifts and savings from actual paid Sunday cover.

steps.text: Keep paid lunch shifts after 2036 and request annual written rate reviews
Save extra cleared Sunday-cover pay toward three months of bills after rent, food and fares

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the owner could remove paid prep before any robot cooks. A written rota, a real posted job if hours are cut and a signed wage after bus fares would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who still checks the chicken board when the office changes the staff list. An empty shift on a screen leaves the same hot kitchen for the people who stay.

headlineQuote: An empty shift on a screen leaves the same hot kitchen for the people who stay.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old certified cook** who leads lunch service, separates raw chicken and watches fridge temperatures.
His **strong kitchen skill** brings a low flat rate, with only two weeks of bills saved and few nearby openings.
He avoids **AI tools** and wants human allergy checks, a written rota and a payslip he can read.
Across the faster pictures he considers **posted cook roles** only after cuts and only for signed replacement net pay.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI picture** could remove paid preparation hours before capable kitchen robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He needs a **written paid rota** and a real qualified opening with signed net pay after bus fares.
